Shallow-water Cape hake (Merluccius capensis) attains a maximum recorded total length of 140 cm [Li = 140 cm], placing it among the larger members of the Merlucciidae family. This ultimate length is typically observed in older females, reflecting the pronounced sexual size dimorphism characteristic of this species. Individuals achieve this size only after many years of growth, supported by a diet that shifts from small crustaceans during the pelagic larval phase to predominantly teleost prey, including anchovy and sardine, in the adult stage. Field surveys along the Benguela Current system have consistently documented these maximum lengths from commercial longline catches, confirming that the species can reach this substantial size under productive upwelling conditions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, estimated from the length-weight relationship, is approximately 23,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 23,000 grams], a figure that underscores the considerable biomass this predator contributes to the demersal fish community. This asymptotic body mass is seldom attained until late in life, reflecting the energy demands of a slow, indeterminate growth strategy.

Female Shallow-water Cape hake typically reach puberty at a total length of 47.4 cm [Lp = 47.4 cm], a size that corresponds closely with the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. At this length, a female's wet weight at puberty is approximately 809 grams [Wwp = approximately 809 grams], derived from the same length-weight relationship applied to the adult population. This length at maturity is relatively modest compared to the ultimate size of 140 cm, indicating that substantial somatic growth continues well after reproductive activity commences. The size threshold for puberty appears influenced by environmental conditions, particularly prey availability and water temperature, with individuals in cooler, more productive regions reaching this length slightly earlier in life. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from captured specimens reveals that females at this length possess developing oocytes, confirming functional reproductive maturity. This early onset of reproduction relative to maximum size is a common strategy among iteroparous gadiform fishes inhabiting variable environments.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Shallow-water Cape hake reaches approximately 20% [GSI = approximately 20%] at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Such a high index is characteristic of batch-spawning teleosts that release multiple egg batches over an extended reproductive period, a strategy that maximizes fecundity in response to variable larval survival conditions. The GSI peaks during the austral winter months, coinciding with the main spawning pulse when mature females aggregate on the continental slope. Spawning adults are typically in good condition, with lipid reserves sufficient to support the metabolic costs of vitellogenesis at this thermal regime.

Fertilised eggs of Merluccius capensis are pelagic and possess a small chorionate embryo encased within a transparent, non-adhesive envelope. At the moment of hatching, following a brief incubation period, the yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], derived from an egg diameter of roughly 900 micrometers. This minute mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva during its initial, non-feeding stage. The newly hatched prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk supply for energy until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins, a critical period during which mortality can exceed 90 percent. The small size at hatching is typical of pelagic-spawning gadoids, trading a higher fecundity per spawn against a lower per-offspring investment. Larval growth during the yolk-sac phase is rapid, with individuals increasing in mass several-fold before the onset of first exogenous feeding on small copepod nauplii.

Under the stable thermal conditions of the Benguela Current, specifically at a sustained temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum lifespan of Shallow-water Cape hake is estimated at approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years]. This longevity, calculated from annuli counts on otoliths, represents the total duration from fertilisation through natural senescence and physiological death. Individuals achieving this age are rare, as fishing mortality removes the majority of the population well before senescence. The lifespan of two decades is consistent with other slow-growing, late-maturing demersal fishes inhabiting cool, productive upwelling zones. At this temperature, metabolic demands are moderate, allowing energy to be allocated toward continued somatic growth and repeated reproductive events over many years. Oldest captured specimens typically display eroded fins, reduced gonadal activity, and signs of physiological deterioration, confirming that natural mortality from senescence occurs near this upper age boundary. Comparative data from related species suggest that 20 years is near the maximum recorded longevity for the genus Merluccius.
